rationale: A wins because it finds the real fourth door: "Toast moves into payroll, betting restaurants haven't solved their tipped-and-hourly wage math." B throws that door away as a "duplicate of the customer-story angle's protagonist," which is just wrong; payroll wage math is not a cash-advance borrower story. Both sets understand the margin and default-rate hooks, but A gives the founder cleaner routes to markets, lending, restaurant-operator, and HR-tech desks.
gaps_in_A: "Toast's profits are coming from lending and payroll" overstates the supplied facts; the update says lending/fintech are higher-margin and Toast reached profitability, not that lending and payroll caused the profit.
"The payroll product is part of the current bundling news — this is the closest thing in the update to a literal launch" is an inference; without a source or date, the 24-hour decay is too confident.
"fees keep piling up" is a useful conflict frame, but it still rests on vague complaints until A gets named owners, fee amounts, and documents.
gaps_in_B: "Toast payroll solves the tipped-vs-hourly staffing headache for operators" refused as "duplicate" is the big miss; payroll/tipped-hourly wage complexity is a separate HR-tech story, not the same borrowing/operator beat.
"The prevailing belief is that a newly profitable, publicly traded platform lending against its own customers' sales has a clean, well-understood book" invents a strawman the update never supplied.

"Next step: newsjack-detector — there is no live news signal in this update" sends the founder sideways; this is already a company update, so reporter fit-checking plus proof-gathering is the right next move.
"because they're higher-margin than the terminals it's known for" smuggles payroll into the margin claim; the update only says lending and fintech are higher-margin than hardware.
